analysis.one_liner: Makes federal agencies prove major rules are the cheapest option and survive trial-style hearings before taking effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Regulatory Accountability Act 253-167 on December 2, 2011, but the Senate committee it went to never acted, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the federal rulemaking process. It would require agencies considering a major rule to publish an advance notice, consult the White House regulatory office, and prove the rule is justified by evidence; it would require agencies to adopt the least costly rule that meets a statutory goal unless they can justify paying more, and to hold trial-style hearings with cross-examination before any rule estimated to cost the economy $1 billion a year or more. It would also let courts throw out an agency's cost-benefit analysis if it did not follow the new guidelines, and stop courts from deferring to agency guidance. In practice, this adds years, hearings, and lawsuits between a public protection and its enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing major federal rules — chemical, energy, manufacturing, financial, and pharmaceutical firms among them — would gain years of delay, hearings, and court challenges to weaken or block rules on health, safety, environment, and consumer protection. The bill's least-costly-rule requirement would also give regulated parties a legal hook to force agencies to pick the cheaper, weaker option.

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to adopt the least costly rule that meets a statute's goals unless they explain why extra benefits justify the extra cost, based on the interests of public health, safety, or welfare.
Any rule estimated to cost the economy $1 billion a year or more could not be adopted until after a formal hearing with a reasonable opportunity for cross-examination of the agency's evidence.
Agencies would have to publish advance notices, consult the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs at OMB, allow 60-120 days of comment, and place everything they considered in a public docket.

Courts could refuse to defer to an agency's cost-benefit analysis if it did not follow the new OMB guidelines, and to agency guidance, and could immediately review interim rules that skipped the new procedures.
Agencies would have to review every major rule at least every ten years to decide whether to keep, change, or repeal it.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal protections — clean air and water, workplace and drug safety, consumer financial rules — would wait longer for new rules and see more of them weakened to the cheapest version, because each added hearing, petition, and lawsuit gives regulated companies another chance to stall or dilute a rule.

drawbacks.text: Requiring the least costly rule that meets a statutory objective shifts the burden onto agencies to defend any stronger protection, pushing them toward weaker versions of safety, health, and environmental rules.
Formal hearings with cross-examination for high-impact rules, new petition rights, and expanded judicial review would let any affected company tie up a major rule in process and litigation for years.

The good-faith case for it: federal rulemaking is slow and opaque, compliance costs fall on businesses and ultimately consumers, and forcing agencies to show evidence, weigh alternatives, and justify costs could produce better-aimed rules and more transparent dockets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency and evidence provisions have real value, and nobody defends wasteful rules. But the bill's core structure points in one direction: a least-costly mandate, trial-style hearings, and expanded court review give regulated companies procedural and legal weapons to delay or dilute rules that protect the public. The cost — years of delay on clean air, drug safety, workplace, and financial protections — falls on the people those rules exist to protect, not on the agencies.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a party-line vote in December 2011, but the Senate committee it was sent to never brought it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Lamar Smith and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on September 22, 2011.
Judiciary ordered the bill reported by a vote of 16-6 on November 3, 2011, and reported it amended on November 22.

Before final passage, Rep. Leonard Boswell moved to send the bill back to committee with an instruction to exempt rules that reduce costs or increase coverage for seniors' pharmaceuticals and health services, including Medicare drug price negotiation; the motion failed 186-233, with 184 of 192 Democrats in favor and 230 of 241 Republicans opposed.
The House passed the bill 253-167 on December 2, 2011: 234 of 241 Republicans voted yes and none voted no, while 167 of 192 Democrats voted no and 19 voted yes.

The Senate received the bill on December 5, 2011 and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which took no further action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agencies kept the existing rulemaking process, so the health, safety, environmental, and financial protections in place at the time were not subject to the new delays and legal challenges; regulated companies were left facing the rules as they were.

for.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through committee hearings, markup, and House floor consideration.

for.name: 234 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage; no House Republican voted against it.

against.name: 167 of 192 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, and 184 of them voted for a motion to exempt senior health and drug-price rules from the bill.

against.name: Rep. Leonard Boswell
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to exempt rules lowering seniors' prescription drug costs; his motion failed 186-233.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Senate committee the bill was referred to (chaired by Joseph Lieberman)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 5, 2011 and never reported it to the Senate floor; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

against.name: Public Citizen and allied consumer, labor, and health groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing its procedures would let regulated industries delay and gut public protections.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split almost entirely by party: 234 of 241 Republicans voted yes with none voting no, while 167 of 192 Democrats voted no and only 19 crossed over; the drug-price motion to recommit split 184 Democrats to 2 Republicans.

industries.industry: Large regulated companies (chemical, energy, utilities, manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill gives them advance notice, hearings with cross-examination, petition rights, and expanded court review, plus a least-costly mandate they can enforce in court. The added years and weaker rules are paid for by the public in the form of delayed health, safety, and environmental protections.

Financial rules costing over $100 million or $1 billion would face the bill's extra procedures, slowing rules on everything from consumer lending to derivatives. The industry's interest in delaying rules runs against the consumers those rules protect.

New hearings, petitions, Information Quality Act challenges, and immediate judicial review create billable work for firms that challenge agency rules. Their revenue comes from the very delay and process that stands between a rule and its enforcement.

Small firms bear real compliance costs and would benefit from slower, cost-tested rules, but unlike large companies they cannot fund years of hearings and litigation, so the bill's procedural advantages flow mostly to deep-pocketed players.
